repos.title: OpenJarvis: Personal AI, On Personal Devices
repos.paper_summary:
**Summary of "Personal AI, On Personal Devices" (OpenJarvis)**

The paper presents OpenJarvis, an architecture that represents a personal AI system as a typed *spec* over five primitives: Intelligence, Engine, Agents, Tools & Memory, and Learning. It also introduces LLM-guided spec search, in which frontier cloud models propose edits to the spec at search time, a held-out gate accepts only non-regressing edits, and the final spec runs entirely on-device. Across eight personal AI benchmarks, the optimized on-device specs match or exceed cloud accuracy on 4 and land within 3.2 pp of the best cloud baseline on average, with roughly 800× lower marginal API cost and 4× lower end-to-end latency. Swapping Claude Opus 4.6 for Qwen3.5-9B in existing stacks drops accuracy by 25–39 pp on PinchBench and GAIA. Prompt optimizers (GEPA, DSPy) close only 5 pp of that gap. Reported gains are averages over 5 runs per configuration, with GPT-5-mini as judge for non-deterministic benchmarks. The authors state that statistical precision is limited by 5 runs per configuration, that judging may be biased, and that evaluation ran on a single machine.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Local models lose 25–39 pp when swapped into cloud-designed personal AI stacks, and prompt tuning recovers only 5 pp.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior tools each formalize part of the stack, and the authors know of no framework jointly evaluating all five primitives.

digest_headlines.heading: Methods
digest_headlines.headline: A typed spec over five primitives lets an LLM proposer edit four of them, keeping only edits that do not regress.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: On-device specs match or exceed cloud accuracy on 4 of 8 benchmarks and land within 3.2 pp of the best cloud baseline on average.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion and Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Frontier models are used only at search time; stated limits include 5 runs per configuration, possible GPT-5-mini judge bias and single-machine evaluation.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers primitive implementation details, cloud-teacher privacy controls, search-phase examples, benchmark descriptions and broader impacts.

repos.title: Unlimited OCR Works
repos.paper_summary: Unlimited OCR is a decoder change to DeepSeek OCR that replaces every decoder attention layer with Reference Sliding Window Attention (R-SWA). Each output token attends to all prefix tokens (visual tokens and the prompt) plus the preceding 128 output tokens, so the KV cache is bounded by prefix length plus 128 rather than growing with output length. The model is continued from the DeepSeek OCR checkpoint for 4,000 steps on about 2M document samples, with the DeepEncoder frozen and 32K-token training sequences. On OmniDocBench v1.5, the overall score rises from 87.01 (DeepSeek OCR) to 93.23. On v1.6, it reaches 93.92, the highest overall score in that table. Decoding throughput is 5580 versus 4951 tokens/s (12.7% higher) at 512 concurrency, measured on short OmniDocBench pages. The paper states that prefill still grows with page count, so the 32K context limits how many pages fit in one pass; the authors plan 128K training.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Current OCR models cannot parse ten pages in one pass, so the paper proposes constant-memory attention for long-horizon parsing.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Works
digest_headlines.headline: Prior end-to-end OCR decoders grow their KV cache with output length, which limits speed and length, so the paper builds on DeepSeek OCR.

digest_headlines.heading: Methodology
digest_headlines.headline: Reference Sliding Window Attention lets each token see all visual and prompt tokens plus the preceding 128 output tokens, keeping the cache constant.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental Settings
digest_headlines.headline: Training uses about 2 million document samples, with synthetic multi-page data, and continues from the DeepSeek OCR checkpoint for 4,000 steps.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: Unlimited OCR scores 93.23 on OmniDocBench v1.5, above DeepSeek OCR's 87.01, and 93.92 on v1.6.

digest_headlines.heading: Efficiency Analysis
digest_headlines.headline: At 6,000 tokens, DeepSeek OCR's generation speed falls 35% behind Unlimited OCR, which keeps a stable rate as output grows.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitation and Future Work
digest_headlines.headline: Unlimited OCR is not truly unlimited because prefill length still grows with page count, so the authors plan longer contexts.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Replacing all decoder attention with R-SWA leaves parsing performance lossless, and the authors expect wider use beyond OCR.

digest_headlines.heading: Author List
digest_headlines.headline: Lists the core contributors and contributors to the Unlimited OCR report, marking the project leader and technical director.

repos.title: AgentScope: A Flexible yet Robust Multi-Agent Platform
repos.paper_summary: AgentScope is a Python-based multi-agent platform that uses message exchange as its core communication mechanism. It provides pipelines and a message hub to structure agent workflows, along with pre-built agents for dialogue, code execution, and image generation. The system handles fault tolerance through service-level retries, rule-based format correction, and customizable handlers for model-resolvable errors. For distributed deployment, an actor-based framework allows developers to use identical workflow code for both local and remote execution without modifying the application logic. Multi-modal data is transmitted via URLs in messages, employing lazy loading to reduce bandwidth overhead during inter-agent communication. A drag-and-drop workstation generates JSON configurations or Python scripts from visual DAGs, enabling non-programmers to build applications. Tool usage follows a ReAct pattern where a service toolkit manages function registration, prompt engineering, and response parsing. The paper does not provide quantitative benchmarks comparing AgentScope against other frameworks like AutoGen or LangChain; instead, it documents architectural features and API interfaces. Limitations include the reliance on LLM capabilities for semantic error detection and the requirement for human intervention when unresolvable errors, such as expired API keys, occur.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Multi-agent application development is hard, so the paper proposes AgentScope, a platform built around message exchange.

digest_headlines.heading: Overview
digest_headlines.headline: AgentScope defines four core concepts (message, agent, service, workflow) and a three-layer architecture.

digest_headlines.heading: High Usability
digest_headlines.headline: Pipelines, a message hub, built-in agents, and a drag-and-drop workstation are offered to reduce development effort.

digest_headlines.heading: Fault-Tolerant Mechanisms
digest_headlines.headline: Errors are sorted into four levels, each handled by retries, rule-based correction, customizable handlers, or logging.

digest_headlines.heading: Multi-Modal Applications
digest_headlines.headline: Multi-modal data is passed as URLs in messages, with files loaded only when needed.

digest_headlines.heading: Tool Usage
digest_headlines.headline: The service toolkit implements a ReAct loop with four steps: function preparation, instructions, reasoning, and acting.

digest_headlines.heading: Agents with Retrieval-Augmented Generation
digest_headlines.headline: Retrieval-augmented generation support uses a one-file configuration and shared knowledge banks that agents can update and weight.

digest_headlines.heading: Actor-based Distributed Framework
digest_headlines.headline: An actor-based distributed mode lets the same workflow run locally or across machines, using placeholder messages.

digest_headlines.heading: Signature Applications of AgentScope
digest_headlines.headline: Example applications include basic and group conversation, a six-player werewolf game, a retrieval-augmented generation copilot, web search, and a database query agent.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Works
digest_headlines.headline: Related frameworks such as LangChain, AutoGen, MetaGPT, and ChatDev are grouped into language agent and multi-agent frameworks.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The paper concludes that AgentScope lowers barriers to multi-agent development and lists RAG and adaptive protocols as future work.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix points to a GitHub repository and lists example dialogue histories for standalone conversation and werewolf.

repos.title: nanoMuse: An Open-Source Personal Agent for Every Device You Own
repos.paper_summary:
nanoMuse is an open-source personal agent that runs on a person’s own devices, including Android and desktop, to act on their accounts and files. It differs from Meta’s Muse by placing the agent directly on user hardware rather than in a cloud VM, providing direct screen control via "Hands," and using file-based memory readable by the user. Every action passes through a Sentinel policy gate that enforces scoped permissions and taint tracking for private data. The system supports multiple LLM providers and uses an optional relay server to sync conversations across devices.

The paper reports estimated resource costs: the Android app is 38 MB, while the desktop app ranges from 256 MB to 498 MB depending on the OS. A self-hosted relay requires approximately 85 MB of idle memory and costs USD 4–6 per month on minimal server tiers. Model usage costs are cited at CNY 2–12 per million tokens. Limitations include the lack of a privilege boundary separating the agent from credentials on a single device, the absence of reported success rates for screen operations, and the fact that memory entries do not yet track provenance or confidence levels.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: A personal agent should be inspectable by its owner, and no open counterpart to Muse existed before this report.

digest_headlines.heading: Personal Agents So Far
digest_headlines.headline: Before September 2026, open personal agents ran on the owner's machine without screens, and screen-operating agents served single tasks.

digest_headlines.heading: How Muse Is Built
digest_headlines.headline: Muse's shape rests on ten visible design choices and safety layers the agent cannot reach, with a virtual machine per person.

digest_headlines.heading: What a Personal Agent Should Be
digest_headlines.headline: A personal agent should answer five questions about memory, action, approval, learning and payment, across three horizons.

digest_headlines.heading: nanoMuse Today
digest_headlines.headline: nanoMuse runs one agent on each device, operating the Android phone's screen and the computer's, with a Sentinel gating every action.

digest_headlines.heading: A Roadmap With the Community
digest_headlines.headline: The open roadmap is set in three distances, from catching up with Muse to an open model for the hands and physical devices.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: nanoMuse's Sentinel shares a trust domain with the agent, and its hands have no measured success rate.

repos.title: OpenHands: An Open Platform for AI Software Developers as Generalist Agents
repos.paper_summary: OpenHands is an open-source platform for building and evaluating AI agents that act on the world by writing code, running shell commands, and browsing the web. Its main components are an event stream that records actions and observations, a Docker-sandboxed runtime with a bash shell, an IPython server, and a Chromium browser, an AgentSkills library of editing and document-parsing tools, and an AgentHub of community agents, including the default CodeAct agent. Agents can delegate subtasks to other agents, and users can add agents or new Docker images. The evaluation framework covers 15 benchmarks, including SWE-Bench, HumanEvalFix, BIRD, and WebArena. The paper reports results across these tasks, but the text provided here does not include the per-benchmark scores, so this summary cannot state them. The platform is released under the MIT license and has 32K GitHub stars and more than 2.1K contributions from over 188 contributors. The paper acknowledges that building agents that are safe and reliable remains an open challenge, which its appendix covers.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: OpenHands is a community platform for building agents that write code, use a shell, and browse the web.

digest_headlines.heading: OpenHands Architecture
digest_headlines.headline: Agents are defined by a step function over an event stream, and actions run in a Docker sandbox that returns observations.

digest_headlines.heading: AgentHub: A Hub of Community-Contributed Agents
digest_headlines.headline: The AgentHub ships a default CodeAct agent, a browsing agent, a graph-based agent, and a template for micro agents.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: Across 15 benchmarks, the CodeActAgent resolves 26% of software engineering issues and fixes 79.3% of Python bugs.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: OpenHands is presented as a community platform that accelerates research and applications of agentic AI systems.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers limitations, ethics, related work, the graphical interface, integration tests, runtime image building, graduate-level benchmark results, prompts, skills, and BrowserGym actions.

repos.title: MOSS-Image Technical Report
repos.paper_summary: MOSS-Image is an open-weight text-to-image system built from a 5B single-stream diffusion transformer (DiT) pretrained from scratch and an intention-aware agentic prompt enhancer that turns short requests into content and layout specifications. The DiT takes text features from a frozen Qwen3.5-9B encoder and latents from a frozen FLUX.2 VAE, and uses 4D RoPE, SiTU-GLU feed-forward layers, and a hybrid Muon–AdamW optimizer. Pretraining uses about 3 billion images after deduplication and AI-image removal, with multi-granularity recaptions, bounding-box JSON annotations, and three resolution stages. The authors introduce LongLongTextBench (LLTB), with 240 English and Chinese literary-text tasks, and RealLayoutArena (RLA), with 61 design requests scored by blind pairwise human comparison on an Elo scale. On LLTB, MOSS-Image scores 96.3 Mean-6, the highest among the open-weight models listed. On 7Bench, it reaches 0.88 `mIoU_det` and 0.70 Layout AUC, versus 0.44 and 0.20 for Ideogram 4. On RLA, it ranks second at 1698.70 Elo, behind GPT Image 2 at 1844.35. Under shared enhanced prompts, its backbone ranks first at 1807.34 Elo. Stated limitations: no reference-image conditioning or editing, and the enhancer depends on external language models.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Open-weight models struggle with dense text, so MOSS-Image pairs a 5B diffusion transformer with an agentic prompt enhancer.

digest_headlines.heading: System Overview
digest_headlines.headline: The system pairs a pretrained text-and-layout renderer with an enhancer that turns concise requests into specifications.

digest_headlines.heading: Pretraining Strategy
digest_headlines.headline: A 5B DiT pretrained from scratch on 3 billion deduplicated images keeps broad data and uses multi-granularity captions.

digest_headlines.heading: Agentic Prompt Enhancement
digest_headlines.headline: An agent routes each request to task guidance and writes structured layouts with literal text, bounding boxes and typography.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: On LLTB, MOSS-Image scores 96.3 Mean-6, and on RLA it ranks second end-to-end at 1698.70 Elo.

digest_headlines.heading: Case Study
digest_headlines.headline: Qualitative cases report that layout prompts enable zero-shot edits, line breaks help text rendering, and zero-centered boxes transfer to unseen resolutions.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Works
digest_headlines.headline: Related work covers foundation models, visual text generation, layout conditioning, prompt agents and text-rich evaluation.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: The backbone cannot condition on reference images or edit images, and the enhancer's errors can reduce specification quality.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: A capable renderer combined with explicit generation specifications supports complex graphics, according to the LLTB and RLA results.

digest_headlines.heading: Contributors
digest_headlines.headline: The contributor list names the project leads, core contributors, other contributors and advisors.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix gives the architecture, training, dataset, filtering, figure and related-work details behind the main text.

repos.title: Codebase-Memory: Tree-Sitter-Based Knowledge Graphs for LLM Code Exploration via MCP
repos.paper_summary:
Codebase-Memory is an open-source system that constructs a Tree-Sitter-based knowledge graph to expose structural code queries to LLM agents via the Model Context Protocol (MCP). The pipeline parses 66 languages, resolves calls using a six-strategy cascade, and detects communities with the Louvain algorithm. It stores the resulting graph in SQLite and exposes 14 typed query tools through a single statically linked C binary with zero runtime dependencies.

Evaluated across 31 real-world repositories, the MCP Agent achieved an 83% answer quality score compared to 92% for a file-exploration agent, while consuming ten times fewer tokens ($\sim$1,000 vs. $\sim$10,000) and requiring 2.1 times fewer tool calls. Query latency was under 1 ms for the MCP agent versus 10–30 s for the explorer. Limitations include reduced accuracy on macro-heavy C code (58% quality) and the absence of source-level context, which requires fallback to file exploration for exhaustive pattern matching.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Text-based code exploration by coding agents scales poorly, so the paper proposes a queryable code knowledge graph exposed via MCP.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work builds heavyweight code graphs or improves agent strategy, leaving the retrieval layer largely unchanged.

digest_headlines.heading: System Design
digest_headlines.headline: Codebase-Memory parses 66 languages into one SQLite knowledge graph and serves it through 14 MCP tools.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: On 31 languages the MCP agent scored 0.83 against 0.92 for the explorer while using 2.1 times fewer tool calls.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Structure helps cross-file queries, but results come from one backend and one repository per language.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The conclusion argues structural retrieval is a viable foundation for LLM-based code intelligence.

digest_headlines.heading: Data Availability Statement
digest_headlines.headline: The source code, benchmark scripts and evaluation data are public for the evaluated release v0.5.5.

repos.title: OpenDataLab: Empowering General Artificial Intelligence with Open Datasets
repos.paper_summary: OpenDataLab is an open data platform and toolchain that standardizes heterogeneous AI datasets using a new specification called Data Set Description Language (DSDL). The system integrates over 6,500 datasets totaling more than 80 TB, including 6 billion images, 1 trillion tokens, and 20,000 hours of audio. DSDL defines a unified syntax for multimodal data representation, allowing users to merge datasets from different sources through a Python SDK or configuration files without manual format alignment. The platform provides a CLI, SDK, and labeling tools (`LabelU` for computer vision tasks and `LabelLLM` for dialogue data) to support the full workflow from download to training. The authors report that this integrated approach improves data preparation efficiency by 30%. A limitation is that the 30% efficiency gain is stated as a general claim without a detailed experimental protocol or baseline comparison in the text. Additionally, while DSDL aims for universality, it currently supports only over 100 standardized datasets, leaving many available formats unconverted.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: OpenDataLab is presented as a five-layer architecture that aims to remove barriers between datasets and processing tools.

digest_headlines.heading: Open Datasets
digest_headlines.headline: OpenDataLab hosts over 6,500 open datasets and records source and license metadata for them.

digest_headlines.heading: Data Set Description Language (DSDL)
digest_headlines.headline: DSDL is a dataset description language designed for universality, portability and extensibility.

digest_headlines.heading: Open Data Platform and Data Toolkits
digest_headlines.headline: The platform adds search, preview, free hosting and download, command-line and Python access, and two labeling tools.

digest_headlines.heading: Use Case
digest_headlines.headline: A worked object detection example merges two datasets with DSDL instead of hand-written alignment code.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: A self-assessed comparison table rates OpenDataLab strong on most dimensions, against weaker ratings for rival platforms.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The authors report a 30% gain in data preparation efficiency, with no experiment shown in the text.

repos.title: DocLayNet: A Large Human-Annotated Dataset for Document-Layout Analysis
repos.paper_summary:
DocLayNet is a publicly available dataset of 80,863 human-annotated PDF pages designed for document layout analysis. The annotations consist of labeled bounding boxes across 11 classes (e.g., Text, Table, Formula) in COCO format. Unlike previous datasets derived from scientific repositories, DocLayNet includes diverse sources such as financial reports and manuals to capture layout variability. A subset of pages contains double or triple annotations to measure inter-annotator agreement.

Baseline experiments using Mask R-CNN, Faster R-CNN, and YOLOv5 show that model performance lags behind human annotation by approximately 10% in mAP@0.5–0.95. Specifically, the best-performing YOLOv5x6 achieves an overall mAP of 76.8%, compared to the human agreement range of 82–83%. A data ablation study indicates that model accuracy plateaus at 80% of the dataset size. Additionally, splitting data on document boundaries rather than individual pages reduces mAP by roughly 10 points, highlighting the risk of overestimation with page-wise splits. Models trained on DocLayNet demonstrate more consistent cross-dataset performance than those trained on PubLayNet or DocBank.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Existing layout datasets come from scientific repositories, so DocLayNet adds human-annotated pages with wider layout variety.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior layout analysis moved from rule-based methods to object detection, and newer text-plus-image models lack a shared data format.

digest_headlines.heading: The DocLayNet Dataset
digest_headlines.headline: DocLayNet contains 80863 pages from six document categories, with 11 labels and pre-defined splits that keep documents whole.

digest_headlines.heading: Annotation Campaign
digest_headlines.headline: Four-phase human annotation under a guideline over 100 pages long improved consistency, though 8 of 40 annotators did not pass.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Baseline detectors trail human agreement by 6 to 10%, and random page-wise splits inflate scores by about 10%.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: DocLayNet supplies human reference metrics and models that transfer better across datasets, yet a gap to humans remains.

repos.title: Mem0: Building Production-Ready AI Agents with Scalable Long-Term Memory
repos.paper_summary: Mem0 is a memory system for LLM agents that extracts, consolidates, and retrieves salient facts from ongoing conversations. Mem0g is a variant that stores those facts as a directed labeled graph of entities and relations. Mem0 runs an extraction phase, which prompts an LLM with a conversation summary, recent messages, and a new message pair to produce candidate facts, and an update phase, which retrieves similar stored memories and has the LLM choose ADD, UPDATE, DELETE, or NOOP through a tool call. On the LOCOMO benchmark, overall LLM-as-a-Judge (J) scores are 66.88% for Mem0 and 68.44% for Mem0g, compared with 60.97% for the best RAG setting and 72.90% for full-context prompting. Mem0 has a p95 total latency of 1.440 s, versus 17.117 s for full-context. Its memory store averages about 7k tokens per conversation, versus about 26k tokens for raw context and over 600k for Zep. Limitations: full-context scores highest on J, Zep leads on open-domain questions, and Mem0g does not improve multi-hop results.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Fixed context windows make AI agents forget user facts across sessions, so the paper proposes persistent memory systems, Mem0 and a graph-based variant.

digest_headlines.heading: Proposed Methods
digest_headlines.headline: Mem0 extracts candidate facts from message pairs and updates memory through add, update, delete or skip decisions; the graph variant stores entities and relations.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental Setup
digest_headlines.headline: The paper tests on the LOCOMO benchmark, scoring answers with lexical overlap metrics and LLM-as-a-Judge against six baseline categories.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation Results, Analysis and Discussion.
digest_headlines.headline: Mem0 leads single-hop and multi-hop questions, the graph variant leads temporal questions, and Zep leads open-domain questions among compared systems.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion and Future Work
digest_headlines.headline: The conclusion claims a balance of accuracy and latency, and names graph operation overhead and non-conversational domains as future work.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists the LLM-as-a-Judge prompt source, has an empty algorithm section, and describes the LoCoMo, ReadAgent, MemoryBank, MemGPT and A-Mem baselines.
